answer:
**In *Proto‑Sino‑Tibetan* the only affixes that Benedict gave their own “chapter‑length” treatment (i.e., a full discussion and reconstruction of their usage in the family) were the six *prefixes* that he reconstructed for the proto‑family.  The chapters are:

| Prefix | Usual gloss in the book | Notable linguistic role |
|--------|-------------------------|------------------------|
| **s‑** | *causative* | Appears throughout Tibeto‑Burman as a causative/motivative prefix; often triggers voice changes. |
| **m‑** | *intransitive / middle* | Used for intransitive verbs and “middle”‑voice marking; often found before the obstruent *s*, *z*, *k*, *g* series. |
| **b‑** | *frequency/continuative* | Recurrent “b‑” prefix seen in many Sub‑Gurung and Qiangic languages, often on verbal stems. |
| **g‑** | *tonic / combative* | Used for “forceful” or “combat” meanings; occurs in a range of Qiangic and Nungish languages. |
| **d‑** | *distributive / spatial* | A prefix found in some Tibeto‑Burman languages giving spatial or distributive meanings. |
| **r‑** | *negative / prohibitive* | The “r‑” negative marker found in a handful of Central Tibetan‑group languages and some Kham dialects. |

These six prefixes are the only ones that Benedict treats in separate, self‑contained chapters; other affixes (e.g., *-s, -t, -n* suffixes and other conditioned forms) are discussed in the general “Morphology” chapter but do not receive their own chapter.

**In *Proto‑Sino‑Tibetan* the only affixes that Benedict gave their own “chapter‑length” treatment (i.e., a full discussion and reconstruction of their usage in the family) were the six *prefixes* that he reconstructed for the proto‑family.  The chapters are:

| Prefix | Usual gloss in the book | Notable linguistic role |
|--------|-------------------------|------------------------|
| **s‑** | *causative* | Appears throughout Tibeto‑Burman as a causative/motivative prefix; often triggers voice changes. |
| **m‑** | *intransitive / middle* | Used for intransitive verbs and “middle”‑voice marking; often found before the obstruent *s*, *z*, *k*, *g* series. |
| **b‑** | *frequency/continuative* | Recurrent “b‑” prefix seen in many Sub‑Gurung and Qiangic languages, often on verbal stems. |
| **g‑** | *tonic / combative* | Used for “forceful” or “combat” meanings; occurs in a range of Qiangic and Nungish languages. |
| **d‑** | *distributive / spatial* | A prefix found in some Tibeto‑Burman languages giving spatial or distributive meanings. |
| **r‑** | *negative / prohibitive* | The “r‑” negative marker found in a handful of Central Tibetan‑group languages and some Kham dialects. |

These six prefixes are the only ones that Benedict treats in separate, self‑contained chapters; other affixes (e.g., *-s, -t, -n* suffixes and other conditioned forms) are discussed in the general “Morphology” chapter but do not receive their own chapter.
